messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

As promised, here is a summary of the solution to my earlier email.  Thank
you to Eric Rexstad for proposing the following resolution. In his words:

" Recognise the tasks you are asking Distance to perform:  estimate a
coefficient associated with a couple of sightings to describe how the shape
of the detection function changes when an unusual glare condition occurs.
Given very little information with which to estimate said coefficient,
Distance complains and fails to converge.

My advice (uninformed by your data) is to build a contingency table
(assuming your covariates are discrete rather than continuous) of the
number of sightings by factor combinations.  That will shed light on the
magnitude of the 'data sparsity' problem.  At that point you might decide
that rather than 3 levels of glare, you recode to only 2 levels.

So the "automatic" nature of 'letting Distance figure it out' begins to
wane; you need to be more elegant in the type of covariate models you
propose and the coding of covariates in your data.  So there is no 'magic
bullet' in a covariate analysis."

As he suggested, I built a contingency table and recognized that a few on
my covariate combinations had only 1 sighting. I then recoded the
problematic variable to correct this issue.  With the newly recoded
variable, I was able to run each candidate MCDS model individually (not
using automated model selection) to select the best model.

I hope this helps anyone with similar data issues.

Best,
Caitlin

messages.body_plain:
Hi Pierre, list,

Thanks for (off the list) answering an additional question, and sending me a
copy of your data.

In my opinion, it's hard to do a robust analysis on your data as sent to me, I'm
afraid.  You have 3 distance bins: 0-0.2km, 0.2-0.55km and 0.55-0.7km units. The
number of observations in these three bins is 1530, 222 and 45 respectively.
So, there's a huge "spike" in detections in the first bin.  Depending on what
model you fit, you can get quite different results with such data.  It would be
much better to have a scenario where either (a) you can be pretty sure you saw
everything in the first bin, and you could treat it as a strip transect; (b) you
saw almost as many things in the second bin as the first, making the results
much less sensitive on the model used.

One thing I note is that the data are multi-species -- are there some species
for which either of the above is true, I wonder.

Now, to your specific question: you fit a model that was half-normal, plus one
cosine adjustment term, plus speed as a continuous covariate, making 3
parameters.  It seems "wrong" that distance will do this, in the sense that
there are only 3 distance bins, so only 3 bits of data.  3 parameters fit to 3
bits of data -- hmm.   However, in fact, there are much more than 3 bits of
data, since each distance recorded at a new value of the continuous covariate
speed provides an extra bit of information for the likelihood.  So, for
covariate analyses, Distance can fit many more parameters than there are
distance bins.  One thing I don't like is that you get no goodness-of-fit under
such circumstances -- we should do something about this at some point.  (Perhaps
it's already fixed in the mrds R package (or Distance package, which uses mrds)
-- I haven't checked.)

One other thing that is evident from your plots is that Distance does not
enforce monotonicity constraints when fitting covariate models, and your fitted
models are quite strongly non-monotonic.  It doesn't use monotonicity because
it's quite a hard problem -- to ensure monotonicity at each level of the
continuous covariate.  Thus, if you really want to include a covariate in your
data, I recommend you consider the mmds package in R, which allows modelling of
detection functions as a mixture of half-normals -- you can include covariates
and all the resulting functions are always monotonic non-increasing.  We have a
submitted paper on this, and the package is available from CRAN.

You also experiment in your Distance project with collapsing two of the bins
into one.  I don't think this will help, so I would not do this.

I hope this is helpful -- I'm happy to correspond more off the list if you like,
and we could post a summary to the list afterwards if necessary.

Cheers Len
